nameStory: This western warbler was named by famous bird artist John James Audubon to honor Scottish ornithologist William MacGillivray, who helped advance the scientific study of birds in the 1800s. Interestingly, Audubon wasn't actually the one who discovered this species - that credit goes to John Kirk Townsend - but Audubon got to do the naming honors anyway!
description: MacGillivray's Warbler is a small, ground-loving songbird that's quite rare in New England, being primarily a western species. These chunky little warblers are olive-green above with sunny yellow bellies, and males sport distinctive black heads that look like they're wearing a dark hood. At about 4-5 inches long with a 7.5-inch wingspan, they're sparrow-sized birds that prefer to stay low in dense vegetation rather than flitting around in treetops like many other warblers. Unlike their hyperactive warbler cousins, MacGillivray's Warblers move deliberately and somewhat sluggishly through the underbrush.

idTips.label: Broken White Eye-rings
idTips.description: Look for distinctive white crescents above and below each eye that form incomplete rings - they look like tiny white eyebrows and under-eye patches that don't quite connect

idTips.label: Male's Black Hood
idTips.description: Breeding males have jet-black heads and upper chests that contrast sharply with their olive backs, creating a dramatic hooded appearance

idTips.label: Female's Gray Head
idTips.description: Females and young birds have soft, drab gray heads instead of black, giving them a more muted but still distinctive appearance

idTips.label: Ground-hugging Behavior
idTips.description: Watch for their sluggish, deliberate movements as they forage low in dense shrubs and undergrowth, rarely venturing high into trees except to sing

idTips.label: Distinctive Song
idTips.description: Listen for their rhythmic 'jeeter jeeter jeeter JEETER JEETER jeet jeet' - a series of two-note phrases that build in volume before ending with two single notes

habitat: In New England, MacGillivray's Warblers are extremely rare vagrants that might occasionally show up during migration in dense, shrubby areas with thick understory vegetation. When they do appear, look for them in overgrown forest edges, dense thickets, or areas with heavy brush and young growth trees where they can stay hidden while foraging.

seasonality.spring: Extremely rare vagrant during spring migration (May), might be found skulking in dense undergrowth. Males would be in their striking black-hooded breeding plumage if encountered.
seasonality.summer: Not expected in New England during breeding season, as they nest in western North America. Any summer sighting would be highly unusual and worth documenting.
seasonality.fall: Slightly more likely than spring but still exceptionally rare during fall migration (September-October). Birds may show duller plumage and be even more secretive than usual.
seasonality.winter: Does not occur in New England during winter months, as these birds migrate to Central America for the cold season.

funFact: MacGillivray's Warblers are so secretive and ground-hugging that they're sometimes called 'feathered mice' by birders - they'll actually scurry along the ground through dense vegetation rather than fly when disturbed, making them one of the most mouse-like birds you might encounter!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Mourning Warbler, but MacGillivray's has those distinctive broken white eye-rings while Mourning Warblers have plain dark eyes with no white markings. Remember: 'MacGillivray's has makeup around its eyes, Mourning Warbler is too sad to bother with eye makeup.'
contextualKnowledge: With only 30 recorded observations in all of New England, seeing a MacGillivray's Warbler here would be like finding a needle in a haystack - they're western birds that very rarely stray this far east. Any potential sighting should be carefully documented and reported to local birding authorities, as it would be a significant regional rarity.
compareHints: Compared to the Common Yellowthroat (the most likely Geothlypis warbler in New England), MacGillivray's is chunkier and more sluggish, lacks the Yellowthroat's distinctive black mask bordered by white, and has those unique broken white eye-rings. The Mourning Warbler is extremely similar but lacks any eye-ring markings and is also very rare in New England, making MacGillivray's broken white eye-rings the key field mark for separating these tricky western vagrants.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common Yellowthroats are the only members of their genus regularly found in New England, making identification easier.
Within its genus, Mourning Warbler is most similar to MacGillivray's Warbler of western North America, but their ranges don't overlap in New England.
Kentucky Warbler is much chunkier and more ground-oriented than its relatives Common Yellowthroat and Mourning Warbler.
